title: Have the AI draw it before it builds it
summary: In three short stops I tell you why drawing matters more now that you do not type the code, give you the one question each of six old drawings answers, and show you how to have the AI draw it for you, agree on it, and save it in the project.

stops.title: The sentence that costs the most

beats.text: You've said this sentence. After the AI builds something fast and sure of itself, exactly to what you described. The problem was the description. When the AI types, the scarce thing is intent, and one sentence carries very little of it.

beats.quote: A drawing is the walk you skipped.
beats.text: When you type code yourself, you learn the shape of it by walking through it. When the AI types it, you skip the walk. A drawing gives it back to you, in a few minutes.

beats.quote: You don't have to draw it.
beats.text:
And here's the good news. You don't have to draw it. The AI is very good at drawing. What matters isn't who held the pen. It's that you and the AI end up with the same picture, written down.

**Beat X**
highlight: why-drawing-matters-more-now | figure: the six drawings and the one question

This is the whole menu on one page. Six drawings, and each one answers exactly one question. You don't need to learn to draw any of them. You need to know which question you're stuck on, so you can ask for the right drawing and tell whether what comes back is right. The next stop takes them one at a time.

beats.quote: the AI generates whatever the code can produce
beats.text: On my own projects I keep a design folder, and the AI generates whatever the code can produce, like the ERD from the database schema. That's heavier than you need. The point is these are old, useful drawings, and you only have to know they exist so you can ask for the right one.

runes.quote: A drawing is the walk you skipped.
A shared, documented understanding is the goal

stops.trial: Think of the last time you said that is not what I meant. Write down what you had not decided yet.
digest: The AI builds what you described, and what you described had holes. A drawing is the walk you skipped, and the AI can draw it for you. What matters is a shared, written-down picture of the plan.

stops.title: Six drawings, one question each

beats.figure: Use case diagram for the portfolio
beats.text: Use case diagram. Who uses it, and what can they do. Draw it before anything else, because it's where you find out you have two kinds of user, not one.

beats.figure: Data flow diagram for the portfolio
beats.text: Data flow. Where does information travel. It's the drawing that shows data moving somewhere you didn't plan. A static portfolio can skip it.

beats.figure: Entity relationship diagram for the portfolio
beats.text: The ERD. What does the thing remember, and how are those things related. For your portfolio, an entry has a date, a title, what you learned, and a link.
Wireframe is gray boxes, on purpose. What goes on each screen, with no one arguing about colors. The mockup is the same thing in real colors and type.

beats.quote: the thousandth screen looks like the first
beats.text: The design system is the reusable parts. I built one, GRAIN, and I'll tell you about it later. The idea is that the thousandth screen should look like the first.

beats.quote: Reach for the one that answers the question
beats.text: You won't need all six. Pick the one that answers the question you can't answer yet, and ask the AI to draw it. Every one has a good tutorial, linked in the note. I'm not teaching them. I'm telling you which one to ask for.

runes.quote: Reach for the one that answers the question

stops.trial: Look at your portfolio brief and name which one of the six answers the question you cannot answer yet. For a portfolio, a use case diagram and a wireframe are plenty.
digest: Use case, who does what. Data flow, where information goes. ERD, what it remembers.
Wireframe, what is on each screen. Mockup, how it looks. Design system, the reusable parts.
You will not need all six. Reach for the one that answers your open question.

stops.title: Let the AI hold the pen

beats.quote: Draw a use case diagram for this.
beats.text: Take the brief from the last lesson, paste it in, and say this. Ask for it as Mermaid, a plain-text way of describing diagrams. Text matters, because you can save it, compare it and change it.

beats.quote: Then read it, and correct it. That's the job.
beats.text: This is your part. The AI draws, you decide. Say, no, a visitor can't add entries, only I can. Each correction costs nothing now. And if you can't tell whether a box is right, ask it to explain that box.

When you both agree, save it in the project, next to your brief. The AI forgets between sessions, so a drawing in the chat is gone tomorrow. A common, written-down understanding is what stops that's not what I meant.

beats.quote: Ask me five questions before you build anything.
beats.text: And the trick from the first lesson. Hand it the drawing and say this. It turns a teammate who guesses into one who checks.

One honest limit, and here I might be wrong about how much you need. A drawing is wrong by the third change if nobody updates it, and a wrong diagram is worse than none. For something tiny, skip all of this. Make them small, and ask the AI to update them.

runes.quote: Ask me five questions before you build anything.

stops.trial: Give your AI your portfolio brief and ask for a use case diagram as Mermaid, then a gray-box wireframe of the roadmap page. Read them, fix one thing, ask what is missing, then save both next to the brief. Or draw it by hand, or draw something stranger.
digest: Describe it and let the AI draw it, ideally in text it can update. Read it and correct it. That is your part.
Save the agreed drawing in the project, so every session works from the same plan.
A drawing is only worth keeping while it matches the code.
